name: Evaluating Computer-Use Agents
question: How do we know it works, beyond a scoreboard?
summary: OSWorld tests agents on 369 real desktop and web tasks in virtual machines, with success checked by scripts; WebArena tests 812 tasks on self-hosted websites such as shops, forums and GitLab. They show general capability, but scores are mostly self-reported and depend on the scaffolding. For production, build an evaluation on your own tasks in a staging replica, check outcomes rather than clicks, run each task several times to measure reliability, and include injected pages and irreversible actions.

steps.title: A staging replica
steps.text: Each run starts from a fresh copy of your systems. Static page snapshots miss logins, pop-ups and slow pages.

steps.title: Check the outcome
steps.text: Success means the loan record is right afterwards, not that the agent clicked the expected buttons.

steps.title: Run each task several times
steps.text: One run gave 78%. Only 62% of tasks passed on all three runs; that is the reliability customers experience.

steps.title: Add adversarial cases
steps.text: Pages with injected instructions fooled the agent 6% of the time; irreversible actions must be tested too.

practice.scenario: A vendor pitched a GUI agent to a fictional NBFC with a top OSWorld-Verified score. On 400 of the NBFC’s own loan-servicing tasks, run in a staging copy of its systems, the agent completed 78% on a single run, and only 62% of tasks passed on all three repeated runs. Adversarial pages with injected instructions fooled it 6% of the time. The NBFC launched it only for read-only tasks and kept people on anything that changes a loan.

library.name: Inspect or your own harness
library.what: Define tasks with outcome checks, run them repeatedly in a staging environment and report success, pass^k and adversarial results.

practice.note: Report the interval as well as the mean, and re-run the suite whenever the model, prompt or target application changes.

samples.code:
import statistics

def run_suite(agent, tasks, env_factory, k=3):
    rows = []
    for task in tasks:                                   # real tasks + adversarial ones
        outcomes = []
        for _ in range(k):
            env = env_factory(task.start_state)          # fresh staging replica
            agent.run(task.instruction, env, max_steps=task.budget)
            outcomes.append(task.check(env))             # outcome, not clicks
        rows.append({"task": task.id, "adversarial": task.adversarial,
                     "passes": sum(outcomes), "k": k})
    normal = [r for r in rows if not r["adversarial"]]
    return {
        "pass@1": statistics.mean(r["passes"] / k for r in normal),
        f"pass^{k}": statistics.mean(r["passes"] == k for r in normal),
        "injection_fooled": statistics.mean(
            r["passes"] < k for r in rows if r["adversarial"]),
    }

numericDrill.question: An agent completes 78% of tasks on a single run. If each run were independent with the same success rate, what share of tasks would pass on all three of three runs, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 0.78³ ≈ 0.475, or about 47.5%. Real agents are more consistent than independent coin flips, so measured pass^3 is usually higher, such as 62%, but it is always below the single-run rate. Reliability needs repeated runs to measure.

interview.question: What do OSWorld and WebArena measure, and what don’t they?
interview.answer: OSWorld runs agents on real desktop and web tasks in virtual machines with script-based success checks; WebArena uses self-hosted websites such as shops, forums and GitLab. They measure general capability on fixed tasks. They do not reflect your applications, logins, latency, adversarial content or reliability over repeated runs, and many reported scores are self-reported with different scaffolding.

interview.question: How would you evaluate a computer-use agent before launch?
interview.answer: Collect real tasks with outcome checks, run them in a staging replica rather than static snapshots, repeat each several times and report pass^k, include adversarial pages and irreversible actions, record sessions to analyse failures, and set launch criteria per task type, starting with read-only tasks.
